questions.question: To perform a diagnostic medial branch block at the L4-5 facet joint, which nerves must be blocked?
options: L4 medial branch and L5 dorsal ramus

wrongAnswerExplanations.0: Each lumbar facet joint receives dual innervation from the medial branch at its own level and the level above. Blocking only one nerve is insufficient.
wrongAnswerExplanations.2: The L4-5 facet joint is innervated by the L3 and L4 medial branches (from the level above and same level), not L4 and L5.
wrongAnswerExplanations.3: The L5 dorsal ramus innervates the L5-S1 facet joint, not L4-5. The L5 dorsal ramus runs in a groove on the sacral ala.

questions.explanation: The L4-5 facet joint receives dual innervation from the L3 medial branch (level above) and the L4 medial branch (same level). This dual innervation principle applies to all lumbar facet joints: the joint is named by its two vertebral levels, and the medial branches come from the upper vertebra's level and one level above that.

rows: Junction of SAP and TP at L3, L4
Junction of SAP and TP at L4, L5
L4 medial branch + L5 dorsal ramus
L5 SAP/TP junction + sacral ala groove

questions.educationalObjective: Each lumbar facet joint has dual innervation from the medial branch at the same level and one level above.

questions.question: A single positive medial branch block with >50% pain relief is sufficient to proceed to radiofrequency ablation.

wrongAnswerExplanations.true: Controlled (dual) diagnostic blocks are the standard. A single block has an unacceptably high false-positive rate (25-40%). The concordant response paradigm requires two separate blocks with consistent relief to establish the diagnosis before proceeding to RFA.

questions.explanation: Dual (controlled) diagnostic blocks are required before radiofrequency ablation. The threshold is typically 80% relief (not 50%) on each block. The dual block paradigm reduces false-positive rates and improves patient selection for RFA, which directly correlates with RFA outcomes.
questions.educationalObjective: Dual concordant medial branch blocks with 80% relief threshold are required before proceeding to radiofrequency ablation.

questions.question: A 72-year-old patient presents with bilateral axial low back pain worse with extension, no radicular symptoms, and MRI showing multilevel facet arthropathy. What is the most appropriate initial diagnostic approach?
options: Proceed directly to bilateral L3-S1 radiofrequency ablation
Order an MRI with contrast to evaluate for infection
Perform diagnostic medial branch blocks at the clinically suspected levels
Trial of lumbar epidural steroid injection

wrongAnswerExplanations.0: RFA should never be performed without prior confirmatory diagnostic blocks. Imaging alone cannot diagnose facet-mediated pain — Dreyfuss showed that clinical exam and imaging have poor sensitivity and specificity for facet pain.
wrongAnswerExplanations.1: There is no clinical indication for infection workup in this presentation. The symptoms are consistent with mechanical facet-mediated pain.
wrongAnswerExplanations.3: The symptoms are axial (not radicular) and worse with extension — this pattern is more consistent with facet pain than radiculopathy. Epidural steroid injections target radicular pain.

questions.explanation: Diagnostic medial branch blocks are the appropriate first step. MRI findings of facet arthropathy do not confirm facet-mediated pain (Dreyfuss demonstrated poor correlation between imaging and symptoms). The patient's age, axial distribution, and extension-aggravated pattern raise clinical suspicion for facet pain, but diagnostic blocks are required to confirm the pain generator before any therapeutic intervention.
questions.educationalObjective: Facet-mediated pain cannot be diagnosed by imaging alone; diagnostic medial branch blocks are required to confirm the pain generator.
